trick: Dimensional analysis is a free check on every formula you write. Both sides of an equation must have the same dimensions, so if they do not, the formula is wrong before you have put a single number in. It cannot prove a formula right, but it catches most mistakes.

video.query: units and measurement dimensional analysis class 11 physics

data.prompt: Match each quantity with its dimensional formula.

trick: Errors add in a fixed way: for a sum or difference you add the absolute errors, for a product or quotient you add the relative errors, and a power multiplies the relative error by that power. So a quantity that is squared contributes twice as much error as one that is not.

video.query: errors in measurement significant figures propagation class 11 physics

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about errors and significant figures.

items.statement: When quantities are added, their absolute errors add.
items.why: Errors never cancel in your favour, so even in a subtraction the absolute errors are added.

items.statement: When quantities are multiplied, their absolute errors add.
items.why: For products and quotients it is the relative or percentage errors that add, not the absolute ones.

items.statement: The number 0.00340 has three significant figures.
items.why: Leading zeros never count; the trailing zero after a decimal point does. So 3, 4 and the final 0.

items.statement: A systematic error can be reduced by taking many readings.
items.why: Repeating readings averages out random error only. A systematic error, like a zero error in the instrument, shifts every reading the same way.

items.statement: If a quantity is squared in a formula, its relative error is doubled.
items.why: A power n multiplies the relative error by n, which is why the most-powered quantity deserves the most careful measurement.

chapter: Motion in a Straight Line and in a Plane
trick: In projectile motion the horizontal and vertical parts are completely independent. Horizontally the velocity never changes; vertically it is ordinary free fall. Solve two simple problems rather than one hard one, and gravity never touches the horizontal.

video.query: projectile motion kinematics equations class 11 physics

data.prompt: Choose the right relation for each case.

items.ask: Velocity after time t under constant acceleration
items.why: The first equation of motion. Check it dimensionally: at is acceleration times time, which is a velocity.

items.ask: Displacement after time t under constant acceleration
items.why: The half belongs to the acceleration term because the extra velocity builds up gradually, so its average contribution is half the final one.

items.ask: Maximum height of a projectile launched at angle θ with speed u
items.why: Height depends only on the vertical component u sinθ. The second option is the range, which uses sin 2θ — the single most confused pair in this chapter.

items.ask: Range of a projectile on level ground
items.why: Range uses sin 2θ, which is why 45° gives the maximum range and why 30° and 60° give the same one. The third option is the time of flight.

trick: Draw the free-body diagram before writing a single equation. Most errors in this chapter are not algebra but a force left off the picture, and the commonest one left off is friction acting against the motion, not along it.

video.query: Newton laws of motion friction free body diagram class 11 physics

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about motion and friction.

items.statement: Newton's third law pair of forces act on two different bodies.
items.why: That is why they never cancel each other. Action and reaction on the same body would leave nothing ever able to accelerate.

items.statement: Limiting friction is greater than kinetic friction.
items.why: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it sliding, which is why an object jerks into motion.

items.statement: Friction depends on the area of contact.
items.why: To a good approximation it depends only on the normal reaction and the nature of the surfaces, not on how much area is touching.

items.statement: A body in uniform circular motion has no acceleration.
items.why: Its speed is constant but its direction changes constantly, so there is a centripetal acceleration directed at the centre.

items.statement: Momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not.
items.why: Momentum is always conserved when no external force acts. It is kinetic energy that is conserved only in an elastic collision.

trick: Work needs a displacement along the force. Carrying a bag horizontally does no work against gravity, because gravity points down and the motion is sideways, and the angle between them is 90 degrees, whose cosine is zero.

video.query: work energy theorem power conservation of energy class 11 physics

data.prompt: Use the work-energy theorem, one step at a time.
data.problem: A 2 kg body at rest is pulled by a constant horizontal force of 10 N over a frictionless floor for 5 m. What is its final speed?

steps.ask: How much work does the force do?
steps.why: W = F × s = 10 × 5 = 50 joules, since the force is along the motion and cos 0° = 1.

steps.ask: By the work-energy theorem, what does that work equal?
steps.why: Net work done equals the change in kinetic energy. This is often quicker than finding the acceleration first.

steps.ask: The body started at rest, so ½mv² = 50. What is v?
steps.why: ½ × 2 × v² = 50 gives v² = 50, so v = √50 ≈ 7.07 m/s. Answering 5 means forgetting to take the square root.

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
trick: Every linear quantity has a rotational twin: mass becomes moment of inertia, force becomes torque, momentum becomes angular momentum, and F = ma becomes τ = Iα. Learn the translations and half the chapter is already familiar.

data.prompt: Match each linear quantity with its rotational counterpart.

trick: Centripetal force is not a new force. It is the name for whatever is already pulling the body towards the centre — tension for a stone on a string, friction for a car on a bend, gravity for a satellite. Always ask which real force is playing that part.
